title: Linear algebra: vectors to decompositions
summary: The language of model representations: vectors, matrices, projections, rank, and singular values.
html:
The language of model representations: vectors, matrices, projections, rank, and singular values.

How the pieces connect

Vectors encode measurements

A vector is an ordered collection of numbers. Its coordinates only have meaning relative to a representation. Addition combines coordinates; scalar multiplication rescales them. The Euclidean norm measures length. A dot product combines coordinatewise products into one value, useful for similarity and linear prediction.

Matrices are linear maps

A matrix maps an input vector to an output vector through weighted sums. Multiplication composes maps. Transposition exchanges rows and columns. An embedding table uses a row lookup, while a neural layer typically multiplies features by a learned weight matrix and adds a bias.

Rank and subspaces

Rank measures the number of independent directions a matrix maps to. Correlated features can reduce effective dimensionality. Orthogonal vectors have zero dot product. Projecting onto a subspace discards information outside it; whether this is useful depends on which information matters for the task.

Decompositions explain compression

The singular value decomposition writes a matrix as UΣVᵀ, separating input directions, strengths, and output directions. Keeping the largest singular values gives a low-rank approximation under standard matrix norms. LoRA parameterizes an update as a product of two thin matrices; it does not require the original matrix to be low rank.

Worked example

For a=[1,2] and b=[3,4], a·b=11. Their norms are √5 and 5, giving cosine similarity 11/(5√5)≈0.984. A large cosine means similar direction in this representation; it is not proof that two sentences make the same claim.

What goes wrong

Similarity depends on the embedding model and normalization. Confusing linear independence with statistical independence mixes two different concepts.

Check your understanding

How many parameters are in a rank-8 update A×B for a 4,096×4,096 weight matrix?

Reveal the explanation

4,096×8 + 8×4,096 = 65,536, compared with 16,777,216 for the full matrix.

An operating model for linear algebra: vectors to decompositions

Linear algebra becomes useful when you read each symbol as a transformation of a space rather than a grid of arithmetic. A row of a weight matrix asks one learned question of an input; a column describes how one input coordinate contributes across outputs. Matrix multiplication composes these questions into layers.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: a recommendation is a projection

Imagine representing a song as a vector whose coordinates encode learned musical properties. A listener history can also be aggregated into a vector. A simple recommender scores each candidate song by a dot product with that history: coordinates aligned with the listener’s preferences add positive evidence; opposed coordinates subtract it. Normalizing vectors turns the score into cosine similarity, which emphasizes direction over magnitude. The model does not need human-readable coordinates for the geometry to matter.

Low-rank structure gives the same system an economic advantage. If a large interaction matrix is well approximated by a few latent directions, the model can store and compute with compact factors instead of one parameter per user–song pair. The caveat is equally important: the approximation preserves the directions favored by the objective, so rare tastes and poorly represented communities can lose detail. A singular-value plot is therefore both an engineering tool and a question about whose variation the system is willing to discard.

Notebook: Check the quantity before trusting it

When reading an equation, annotate every object with its shape and ask what each axis means. If a multiplication has no interpretation in terms of mapping or aggregation, the notation has become disconnected from the model.

import numpy as np
x = np.array([2., -1.])
W = np.array([[1., 3.], [0., -2.]])
y = W @ x
print("shape", y.shape, "value", y)
# Write units and axis meanings beside every array.
What to test next. 1. Represent: Choose coordinates, shapes, and a basis. 2. Transform: Apply a matrix as a linear map. 3. Measure: Use dot products, norms, projections, and rank. 4. Compress: Retain useful directions with low-rank structure.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Represent. Choose coordinates, shapes, and a basis.
  2. Transform. Apply a matrix as a linear map.
  3. Measure. Use dot products, norms, projections, and rank.
  4. Compress. Retain useful directions with low-rank structure.

The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority.

Vectors represent states, not arrows by default

A vector is an element of a space whose operations obey specific rules. Coordinates appear only after choosing a basis. The same abstract vector can have different coordinate lists in different bases, which is why a basis change can expose structure without changing the represented object.

  • Vector spaces define legal combination. Addition combines states and scalar multiplication changes scale. Images, audio windows, token embeddings, model parameters, and probability tables can all be vectors once their coordinate assumptions are explicit.
  • A basis is a coordinate system. Basis vectors span the space and remain linearly independent. Every vector has one coordinate representation in that basis. Learned representations choose coordinates that make downstream transformations useful.
  • Subspaces describe constrained variation. The column space contains outputs a matrix can produce. The null space contains inputs erased by the transformation. Rank counts independent directions preserved by the map.
  • Affine operations add translation. A neural layer usually computes Wx+b. The matrix is linear; the bias shifts the origin. Calling the whole layer linear is common shorthand but mathematically imprecise.

The gotcha. A coordinate has no stable meaning outside its basis. Comparing individual embedding dimensions across independently trained models usually has no invariant interpretation.

Matrix multiplication composes transformations

If A maps inputs into an intermediate space and B maps that representation into an output space, BA performs both maps in order. The shared inner dimension is the interface contract. Order matters because matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.

  • Rows ask questions. Each row forms a dot product with the input. It measures alignment with one learned direction and becomes one output coordinate.
  • Columns show contribution. A column describes how one input basis direction influences every output coordinate. Reading rows and columns this way turns a grid of numbers into a map between representations.
  • Batched multiplication adds leading axes. Libraries apply products across batches, heads, or spatial positions. Shape notation should identify these axes because broadcasting can replicate a matrix without copying it.
  • Associativity creates implementation choices. A(BC) and (AB)C are mathematically equal when shapes allow, but intermediate sizes and rounding differ. Compilers choose contraction orders to reduce work or memory.

The gotcha. Compatible shapes do not guarantee a correct semantic contraction. Label every axis before trusting a high-rank tensor expression.

Inner products create geometry

An inner product turns two vectors into a scalar and defines length, angle, and orthogonality. The ordinary dot product is one inner product. Other positive-definite forms encode different geometry by weighting directions differently.

  • Norms measure size. The Euclidean norm follows from the dot product. L1 and max norms measure different properties and induce different nearest points. Regularization and robustness claims depend on the selected norm.
  • Cosine similarity removes magnitude. Dividing a dot product by both norms measures directional alignment. It is undefined for a zero vector and can hide confidence or frequency information stored in magnitude.
  • Projection finds the represented component. Orthogonal projection decomposes a vector into a component inside a subspace and a perpendicular residual. Least squares uses this geometry when no exact solution exists.
  • Gram matrices collect pairwise products. XᵀX records feature relationships; XXᵀ records sample relationships. Forming either explicitly can square a large dimension and worsen conditioning.

The gotcha. Similarity in an embedding space comes from the training objective and data. Proximity does not automatically mean factual equivalence, causality, or fairness.

Linear systems and least squares

The equation Ax=b asks for an input whose transformation equals the target. A unique solution requires the map to preserve enough independent directions. When observations conflict or outnumber parameters, least squares minimizes the squared residual norm.

  • Elimination reveals structure. Row operations preserve the solution set while reducing a system to triangular form. Pivoting avoids division by dangerously small values and improves numerical behavior.
  • Overdetermined systems project. Least squares projects b onto the column space of A. The residual is orthogonal to every column, yielding the normal equation AᵀAx=Aᵀb.
  • Normal equations can be unstable. Forming AᵀA squares the condition number and can lose precision. QR or SVD costs more arithmetic but preserves more numerical information.
  • Regularization changes the question. Ridge regression adds a parameter-norm penalty. It stabilizes poorly determined directions while introducing bias, creating an explicit bias-variance tradeoff.

The gotcha. Never form a matrix inverse merely to solve a system. Use a factorization that exploits structure and reports numerical failure.

Decompositions expose useful axes

A decomposition rewrites one transformation as simpler factors. The factors reveal directions, scaling, rotation, triangular structure, or low-rank approximation and usually provide a better computational route than direct symbolic manipulation.

  • QR separates orientation and scale. An orthogonal factor preserves lengths while a triangular factor supports efficient substitution. QR is a reliable default for least squares.
  • Eigenvectors describe invariant directions. An eigenvector keeps its direction under a square transformation while its eigenvalue gives the scale. Defective or non-normal matrices may lack a stable eigenbasis.
  • SVD works for rectangular matrices. Singular value decomposition expresses a map as orthogonal input directions, nonnegative scales, and orthogonal output directions. Truncation gives the best low-rank approximation under common norms.
  • Condition number predicts sensitivity. The ratio of largest to smallest relevant singular value estimates how much input or rounding error can be amplified. A formally solvable equation can still be unreliable.

The gotcha. A small singular value may represent noise or a rare but essential direction. Validate compression on the downstream task, not only reconstruction error.

Attention is linear algebra with data-dependent weights

A transformer projects token representations into queries, keys, and values. Query-key dot products create pairwise scores. Softmax turns each row into nonnegative weights summing to one, and a weighted sum of values produces a context-dependent representation.

  • Projection defines comparison spaces. Learned matrices decide which features queries ask for, keys advertise, and values transmit. Multiple heads repeat the process in smaller subspaces.
  • Scaling controls magnitude. Dividing scores by the square root of head width keeps their variance from growing with dimension under common initialization assumptions.
  • Masking changes legal interactions. A causal mask prevents positions from using future tokens. Padding masks remove nonexistent positions. A mask bug can leak answers while training loss looks excellent.
  • Output projection mixes heads. Concatenated head outputs return through a learned map to model width. Residual paths and normalization then change both representation and optimization behavior.

The gotcha. Attention weights are internal routing coefficients. They are not automatically faithful explanations of what caused the final prediction.

A numerical checklist for linear algebra code

  • Annotate shapes and axes. Record the semantic role of every dimension beside equations and assertions.
  • Track dtype and device. Know where conversion, copying, accumulation, and synchronization occur.
  • Avoid explicit inverses. Choose a solver matched to symmetry, sparsity, definiteness, and conditioning.
  • Measure residuals. Check both forward error and how well the computed result satisfies the original equation.
  • Test invariants. Orthogonal matrices preserve norms; probability rows sum to one; covariance matrices should remain symmetric positive semidefinite within tolerance.
  • Use tiny exact cases. Compare optimized kernels against hand-computed examples before scaling dimensions.

The gotcha. A result can have the expected shape, finite values, and low runtime while remaining mathematically wrong because one axis, transpose, or normalization convention was misidentified.
